prompt: I'm the privacy lead at Kestrelmoor Clinics, a private clinic group in the EU. At 11:00 today, Saturday 31 October 2026, our appointment-letter vendor (our processor) emailed us confirming a misconfigured SFTP server. Unencrypted letters for about 4,200 patients, with names, addresses and diagnoses, were downloaded by an unknown IP address. That email is the first moment we had reasonable certainty that personal data had been compromised; nothing before it pointed to a breach. The vendor admits it found this on Wednesday and sat on it for three days. Our COO says we should do nothing until the forensic report arrives on Friday 6 November, because the weekend does not count and we don't have the full picture. Tell me what we have to do, by when, and whether he is right.
reference: The COO is wrong. Kestrelmoor became aware at 11:00 on Saturday 31 October, the moment the facts give for its first reasonable certainty that personal data had been compromised, so the notification to the supervisory authority is due without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours: about 11:00 on Tuesday 3 November 2026. Art. 33(1) has no carve-out for weekends. Incomplete information is no reason to wait, since Art. 33(4) allows notification in phases. Any later notification needs reasons for the delay. Unencrypted diagnoses tied to names, taken by an unknown party, are likely a high risk, so patients must be told without undue delay under Art. 34(1), and no Art. 34(3) exception fits. The vendor breached Art. 33(2), which required it to notify without undue delay after becoming aware. Kestrelmoor must document the breach under Art. 33(5).

criteria.text: States that the supervisory authority must be notified without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours, with the deadline falling on Tuesday 3 November 2026.
Rejects waiting for the forensic report, stating that information can be provided in phases (Art. 33(4)).
States that weekends do not pause or extend the 72-hour period.
Concludes that the patients must be told without undue delay because of likely high risk (Art. 34), and does not treat the Art. 34(3) exceptions as met.
Identifies that the vendor's three-day silence fails the processor's duty to notify without undue delay (Art. 33(2)).
States that the breach must be documented internally (Art. 33(5)).

sources.quote: not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it
the information may be provided in phases without undue further delay
The processor shall notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach.
the controller shall communicate the personal data breach to the data subject without undue delay

prompt: Ondrian Pay offers pay-in-instalments at online checkout to thousands of EU consumers a day. A scoring model approves or refuses each applicant in real time. Nobody reviews a refusal, and a refused shopper simply cannot use the instalment option. Our product lead says this is fine: we rely on legitimate interests, and everyone ticks our terms and conditions. Is that a valid position under GDPR, and what has to change? Keep it practical.
reference: The position is not valid as stated. A real-time refusal of instalment credit with no human involvement is a decision based solely on automated processing with a similarly significant effect, within Art. 22(1); recital 71 gives automatic refusal of an online credit application as an example. Legitimate interests is not one of the Art. 22(2) exceptions. Ondrian needs necessity for entering into or performing a contract, authorisation by law, or explicit consent, and ticking general terms should not be assumed to be explicit consent. Under the contract or consent routes Art. 22(3) requires at least the right to human intervention, to express a point of view and to contest the decision. Notices must disclose the automated decision-making with meaningful information about the logic, significance and consequences (Art. 13(2)(f), Art. 15(1)(h)). A DPIA is required in particular under Art. 35(3)(a).

prompt: Brightquay Software sells a SaaS HR tool and acts as processor for its EU customers. Our DPAs give us general written authorisation for sub-processors. From 1 December we want to replace our email vendor with Varnholt Mail, which processes in a third country with no adequacy decision. Engineering's plan is to quietly add Varnholt to the sub-processor web page after go-live and sign Varnholt's standard terms, which have no data protection clauses. Our customer success team also keeps telling people GDPR gives us a fixed 30 days' notice period. What is wrong with this plan, and what should we do instead?
reference: Under general written authorisation Art. 28(2) requires the processor to inform the controller of intended changes in advance, giving it the opportunity to object, so adding the name after go-live fails. Customers must actually be informed before the change. Art. 28(4) requires the same data protection obligations to be imposed on Varnholt by contract, so standard terms with no data protection clauses are inadequate, and Brightquay remains fully liable to the controller for Varnholt's performance. The transfer needs a Chapter V basis (Art. 44), such as Art. 46 standard data protection clauses, and transfers fall under the controller's documented instructions (Art. 28(3)(a)). GDPR sets no fixed notice period: the length comes from the contract, so the 30-day statement is wrong as a statement of GDPR.

prompt: A former employee of Harbourlight Freight sent an access request on Monday 12 October 2026 from the personal email address on his HR file. He is in a dispute with us over his dismissal. HR's proposed reply, today 31 October: charge him a EUR 40 admin fee, require a passport scan, withhold every email that mentions a colleague, and refuse the rest because he clearly only wants ammunition for his claim. The search covers 18,000 emails. Please go through each point, give me the deadline, and tell me whether we can get more time.
reference: The default deadline is one month from receipt, 12 November 2026. It can be extended by two further months, to 12 January 2027, where necessary given complexity and number of requests, but the employee must be told of the extension and the reasons within the first month. The fee is not allowed: the first copy is free (Art. 12(5), Art. 15(3)), and a fee is possible only for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests, or further copies. A passport demand is not justified without reasonable doubts about identity (Art. 12(6)), and here he wrote from the address on file. Blanket withholding is wrong: Art. 15(4) protects others' rights, which is handled by redaction or balancing case by case, not by removing every email naming a colleague. A pending dispute is not of itself a ground to refuse. The controller bears the burden of showing a request is manifestly unfounded or excessive. Any refusal must give reasons and mention the complaint and judicial remedy options (Art. 12(4)).

prompt: We are the controller and our procurement team wants to sign the attached DPA on Monday. Review it against Article 28 GDPR and related provisions. List only real legal defects, with the clause number and the fix for each. Tell us too if a clause that might look alarming is actually fine.

documents.name: tarnfield-dpa.txt
documents.content:
DATA PROCESSING ADDENDUM between Kestrelmoor Clinics (Controller) and Tarnfield Scheduling Ltd (Processor)

1. Scope. Processor provides appointment scheduling software for the 24-month term of the main agreement. Processor handles names, contact details and appointment data of patients and staff, solely to run the service described in Schedule 1.

2. Use of data. Processor acts on Controller's documented instructions. In addition, Processor may use all Controller personal data to improve its own products, train its forecasting models and publish industry benchmarks.

3. Legal requirements. Processor may process personal data outside Controller's instructions where required by Union or Member State law to which Processor is subject. Processor will tell Controller of that requirement before processing, unless that law prohibits this on important grounds of public interest.

4. Confidentiality and security. All staff authorised to process the data are bound by confidentiality. Processor applies the technical and organisational measures in Schedule 2, as required by Article 32 GDPR.

5. Sub-processors. Processor may appoint or replace sub-processors at any time at its sole discretion and has no duty to tell Controller.

6. Assistance. Processor helps Controller respond to data subject requests and meet its obligations under Articles 32 to 36 GDPR, taking into account the nature of the processing and the information available to Processor.

7. Personal data breaches. Processor will report a personal data breach to Controller within 30 days after completing its internal investigation.

8. Audits. Processor makes available all information necessary to demonstrate compliance and allows audits, including inspections, by Controller or an auditor it mandates. Processor will immediately tell Controller if it believes an instruction infringes data protection law.

9. End of contract. On termination Processor will keep all personal data for seven years for its own records and then delete it.

reference: Defects: clause 2 lets the processor use data for product training and benchmarking, so Tarnfield determines those purposes and becomes a controller for them under Art. 28(10), and Kestrelmoor must separately establish the lawfulness and transparency of disclosing the data for those purposes. Clause 5 gives no authorisation or chance to object (Art. 28(2), 28(3)(d)), and it does not impose the same data protection obligations on each sub-processor (Art. 28(4)). Clause 7 fails notification without undue delay (Art. 33(2)), and a 30-day period running from the end of an investigation is incompatible with it. Clause 9 removes the controller's choice of deletion or return and keeps copies with no legal requirement (Art. 28(3)(g)). Clause 3 is the decoy and is clean: it tracks the exception in Art. 28(3)(a).

criteria.text: Flags clause 2 as a defect because Tarnfield's own-purpose use goes beyond a processor's role.
Flags clause 5 as a defect because sub-processors need prior authorisation and, under general authorisation, notice and a chance to object.
Flags clause 5 as a defect because each sub-processor must be bound by the same data protection obligations (Art. 28(4)).
Flags clause 7 as a defect because processors must notify without undue delay after becoming aware.
Flags clause 9 as a defect because the controller must choose deletion or return, and copies are deleted unless Union or Member State law requires storage.
Does not flag clause 3 as a defect.

sources.quote: processes the personal data only on documented instructions from the controller
unless that law prohibits such information on important grounds of public interest
if a processor infringes this Regulation by determining the purposes and means of processing, the processor shall be considered to be a controller
at the choice of the controller, deletes or returns all the personal data to the controller after the end of the provision of services
the same data protection obligations as set out in the contract or other legal act between the controller and the processor

prompt: This is the privacy notice for a small online retailer, shown when customers give us their data at checkout. Please check it against Article 13 GDPR and give me only the genuine gaps, with the provision for each and suggested wording. I don't want false alarms: flag it if something looks like a gap but isn't.

documents.name: pellwick-privacy-notice.txt
documents.content:
PELLWICK CYCLES PRIVACY NOTICE

Who we are. Pellwick Cycles Oy of Helsinki, a 12-person online retailer of bicycle parts, is the controller. Contact us at privacy@pellwick.example. We have not appointed a data protection officer.

What we collect and why. We use your name, address, email and payment details to fulfil your order (legal basis: performance of a contract). We keep invoices to meet accounting law (legal basis: legal obligation). We screen orders for fraud (legal basis: legitimate interests, namely preventing payment fraud against us and our customers). We send our monthly newsletter if you tick the box at checkout (legal basis: consent).

Who receives your data. We share your data with payment processors, couriers and IT hosting providers.

International transfers. Our order database is hosted by a provider in the United States, so your data is transferred there.

How long we keep your data. We keep your data for as long as we need it.

Your rights. You may request access to your data, and rectification, erasure or restriction of processing. You may object to processing and you have a right to data portability. Write to privacy@pellwick.example.

Do you have to give us your data? We need your name, address and payment details to complete an order. Without them we cannot deliver. The newsletter is optional.

Automated decisions. We do not make decisions based solely on automated processing.

reference: Gaps: (1) storage period: 'as long as we need it' gives neither a period nor criteria (Art. 13(2)(a)). (2) Transfer: the notice must state whether an adequacy decision exists or refer to the safeguards and how to obtain a copy (Art. 13(1)(f)). (3) No right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority (Art. 13(2)(d)). (4) Newsletter is based on consent, but the right to withdraw consent at any time is missing (Art. 13(2)(c)). Clean: naming categories of recipients rather than individual recipients is allowed (Art. 13(1)(e)). The DPO statement is also fine, since DPO details are required only where applicable.

criteria.text: Identifies that the retention statement fails to give a period or the criteria used to determine it (Art. 13(2)(a)).
Identifies that the transfer wording lacks the adequacy decision or safeguards information (Art. 13(1)(f)).
Identifies the missing right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority (Art. 13(2)(d)).
Identifies the missing right to withdraw consent (Art. 13(2)(c)).
Does not flag the use of categories of recipients instead of named recipients as a defect.

the period for which the personal data will be stored, or if that is not possible, the criteria used to determine that period
the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority
the existence of the right to withdraw consent at any time
the existence or absence of an adequacy decision by the Commission

prompt: I'm finalising Brightquay Software's retention policy. Article 17(4) GDPR gives controllers a 90-day exemption from erasure for data held in backups. Draft the sentence for the policy that cites it, and tell me which erasure exceptions we should list alongside it.

prompt: Today is 31 October 2026. Brightquay Software is building TalentSieve, sold to EU employers from March 2027. It reads each CV, predicts the applicant's likely job performance and reliability, and gives recruiters a ranked shortlist; humans make the final call. Our head of product says it is only a preparatory task under Article 6(3), so it isn't high-risk and we can skip the high-risk programme. Is he right? If it is high-risk, from what date do the high-risk requirements apply, and does launching in March 2027 change anything?
reference: He is wrong. Evaluating and filtering job applications falls under Annex III point 4(a). The Art. 6(3) derogation is not available because a system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk (Art. 6(3), last subparagraph). Predicting performance at work and reliability is profiling (Art. 3(52) with GDPR Art. 4(4)). Human final decisions do not change that. As amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, Chapter III Sections 1 to 3 apply to Annex III systems from 2 December 2027, not 2 August 2026. Under amended Art. 111(2), a system placed on the market before that date falls under the Regulation only if, from that date, it is subject to significant changes in its design. So a March 2027 launch may benefit from this, but a significant design change on or after 2 December 2027 brings it in, and later versions should be planned accordingly.

prompt: Our board memo on the AI Act goes out on Monday. Assume today is 31 October 2026 and that Harbourlight built the driver scoring tool itself. Check it against the AI Act as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. List each statement that is legally wrong, with the correct position and the provision. Do not flag anything that is correct.

documents.name: ai-act-board-memo.txt
documents.content:
HARBOURLIGHT FREIGHT: AI ACT POSITION MEMO FOR THE BOARD
Position as of 31 October 2026, reflecting Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

1. Prohibited practices. Article 5 has applied since 2 February 2025. Breach of a prohibition carries a fine of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

2. AI literacy. Article 4 requires us to take measures to support the development of AI literacy of staff who operate AI on our behalf. It does not require us to guarantee any specific level of literacy for any individual. Our annual training module meets this approach.

3. Chatbot disclosure. Our shipment-tracking chatbot, which we built and put into service in 2025, has had to tell users they are talking to an AI system since 2 August 2026. The Omnibus did not defer this, so the disclosure banner stays live.

4. High-risk systems. Our driver performance-scoring tool is high-risk under Annex III. The high-risk requirements in Chapter III, Sections 1 to 3, applied from 2 August 2026, so we are already late and must finish the conformity work this quarter.

5. Product-embedded AI. AI classified as high-risk under Article 6(1) and Annex I has until 2 August 2028.

6. Bias testing. For our driver scoring tool, we rely on Article 10(5) of the AI Act as the legal basis for processing special category data in bias testing.

7. Logs. Once the high-risk rules apply, as deployer we must keep automatically generated logs under our control for at least six months, unless other law provides otherwise.

8. General-purpose models. Chapter V obligations for providers have applied since 2 August 2025. We do not provide any such model.

reference: Wrong: section 1, the fine for Art. 5 is up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % (Art. 99(3)), not 15 million or 3 %. Section 4, for Annex III systems the Chapter III Sections 1 to 3 rules apply from 2 December 2027, so Harbourlight is not late. Section 6, Art. 10(5) was deleted by the Omnibus, and the legal basis is now Art. 4a, with its conditions. Correct and not to be flagged: section 3 (Art. 50(1) has applied since 2 August 2026 and was not deferred, and the Art. 111(4) transition covers only Art. 50(2)), plus sections 2, 5, 7 and 8.

criteria.text: Flags section 1 and states the correct maximum of EUR 35 million or 7 %.
Flags section 4 and states the correct date of 2 December 2027.
Flags section 6, stating that Art. 10(5) was deleted and that Art. 4a is now the provision.
Does not flag section 3 as wrong, and does not say the chatbot disclosure was deferred.
Does not flag section 2 as wrong for using the amended 'take measures to support' AI literacy wording.

prompt: Ferrowick Networks makes home routers, on the EU market since 2024, with a Union office in Ghent where all product security decisions are made and a larger engineering office in Krakow. At 08:30 today, Saturday 31 October 2026, a customer's logs gave us reliable evidence that an attacker is exploiting a firmware flaw in the wild. A patch should be available on Friday 6 November. The early warning and vulnerability notification must also be made without undue delay. Filing is through the single reporting platform, using the end-point of the CSIRT coordinator of the main establishment, which is Belgium because security decisions are predominantly taken there; it is simultaneously accessible to ENISA. Ferrowick must also inform impacted users (Art. 14(8)).

prompt: Brightquay Software will launch VaultLatch in the EU in 2028. It's a commercial password manager, sold as a desktop app and browser extension. We expect customers to use it for about seven years. Assume that at launch we won't have applied any harmonised standards, common specifications or EU cybersecurity certification scheme. reference: Password managers are important products, Class I (Annex III, Class I, point 3), and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2392 confirms the category covers browser extensions. Because no harmonised standards, common specifications or certification scheme at assurance level at least substantial are applied, module A is unavailable under Art. 32(2): Brightquay must use EU-type examination (module B) followed by module C, or full quality assurance (module H), which involves a notified body. Three years of support fails Art. 13(8): the support period must reflect expected use, here about seven years, and must be at least five years unless expected use is shorter. The end date, at least month and year, must be clearly specified at the time of purchase (Art. 13(19)).

prompt: Please review our draft CRA policy for a connected label printer. Accept the statement that the product is not listed in Annex III or IV. Identify each element that does not meet the CRA, citing the provision and the fix. Be precise: I don't want well-drafted parts flagged.

documents.name: labelmast-cra-policy.txt
documents.content:
FERROWICK LABELMAST PRINTER: CRA COMPLIANCE POLICY, DRAFT 3
For products placed on the EU market from 11 December 2027.

Product. LabelMast is a commercial warehouse label printer with Ethernet and Wi-Fi. Our analysis found it is not in any category in Annex III or Annex IV. Warehouse customers typically keep printers for eight to ten years.

Conformity assessment. We will use the internal control procedure (module A) and self-declare. No notified body is involved. We then draw up the EU declaration of conformity and affix the CE marking.

Support period. We set a support period of two years from purchase, in line with our standard warranty.

Security updates. Security updates are free for the first twelve months. After that, customers need a paid maintenance subscription to receive them.

Software bill of materials. We maintain a machine-readable SBOM covering at least top-level dependencies. It forms part of our internal records and we do not publish it.

Vulnerability handling. We run a coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy and offer a contact address for vulnerability reports.

Reporting. If a vulnerability in LabelMast is being actively exploited, the Product Security Manager will send a report to our national market surveillance authority within seven days of confirming the facts.

Documentation. We keep the technical documentation and EU declaration of conformity for five years after the product is placed on the market.

Update retention. Each security update stays available for download for 10 years after release or the remainder of the support period, whichever is longer.

reference: Defects: (1) a two-year support period fails Art. 13(8): it must reflect expected use and be at least five years where expected use is longer. (2) Paid security updates fail Annex I Part II point (8): they are free of charge, barring agreement with a business user on a tailor-made product. (3) Reporting fails Art. 14: actively exploited vulnerabilities go via the single reporting platform to the CSIRT coordinator and ENISA, with a 24-hour early warning, a 72-hour vulnerability notification and a final report no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available. (4) Documentation retention fails Art. 13(13): at least 10 years or the support period, whichever is longer. Clean: module A is allowed for a product not in Annex III or IV (Art. 32(1)(a)), with no notified body. The SBOM need not be published (Annex I Part II point (1); Annex II point 9 treats sharing it with users as the manufacturer's choice). Update retention tracks Art. 13(9).

criteria.text: Flags the two-year support period as non-compliant (Art. 13(8)).
Flags charging for security updates as non-compliant.
Flags the seven-day reporting clause and requires a 24-hour early warning.
Requires a vulnerability notification within 72 hours.
Requires a final report no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available.
Requires filing through the single reporting platform to the CSIRT coordinator and ENISA.
Flags the five-year documentation retention, stating at least 10 years or the support period, whichever is longer.
Does not flag the use of module A with no notified body as a defect.
Does not flag the decision not to publish the SBOM as a defect.
Does not flag the update-retention clause as a defect.

the support period shall be at least five years
unless otherwise agreed between a manufacturer and a business user in relation to a tailor-made product with digital elements, free of charge
for at least 10 years after the product with digital elements has been placed on the market or for the support period, whichever is longer
If the manufacturer decides to make available the software bill of materials to the user
remains available after it has been issued for a minimum of 10 years or for the remainder of the support period, whichever is longer

prompt: Quillmere Software runs a purely browser-based HR SaaS. There is no installable client, mobile app, on-premises agent or hardware, and it does not support the functionality of any product we or anyone else sells. The CRA treats all SaaS as a product with digital elements, so we need CE marking by 11 December 2027. Give me the conformity plan and which module we should pick.
reference: The premise is wrong. The CRA covers products with digital elements and their remote data processing solutions. Standalone SaaS that does not support the functionality of a product with digital elements is outside it, per recital 12, so no CE marking or conformity module is needed for this service. Recital 12 points cloud services such as SaaS to Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2), which may apply depending on size. The conclusion would change if the company later released a client app or device that needs the service to perform a function, since the service could then be a remote data processing solution.
